title: Quantitative CT definition of solid components in pulmonary ground-glass nodules: a pixel-level annotation-based development and internal validation study.
abstract: Background Solid-component assessment in pulmonary ground-glass nodules (GGNs) remains subjective, and no universally accepted computed tomography (CT) attenuation threshold exists. Fixed cutoffs may not account for inter-lesion variation in baseline ground-glass opacity (GGO) attenuation. We aimed to develop and internally validate lesion-adaptive quantitative CT definitions of the solid component using three-dimensional pixel-level expert annotations as the imaging reference standard. Methods This retrospective single-center methodological study included 170 unique patients with 170 surgically resected stage I lung adenocarcinoma-spectrum GGNs from March 2015 through July 2018 and each patient contributed one target lesion. All examinations were acquired on the same 256-row CT scanner, and venous-phase 1-mm images reconstructed with medium-strength deep learning image reconstruction were used for analysis. Each lesion was independently annotated by at least two experienced thoracic surgeons, with Dice-based adjudication and senior review. Patients were randomly allocated to training (n=120) and internal validation (n=50) cohorts. Nine prespecified study methods and three literature-based fixed thresholds were evaluated at pixel and lesion levels. Results The training and validation cohorts had median lesion sizes of 1.2 and 1.3 cm and median annotated solid-component proportions of 0.324 and 0.319, respectively. The GGO mean plus ratio method achieved the highest area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve [AUC, 0.848; 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.841-0.856], with sensitivity of 0.732, specificity of 0.815, and F1/Dice of 0.760. The GGO mean plus difference method yielded the highest lesion-level coefficient of determination (R 2 , 0.744; 95% CI: 0.499-0.889), whereas the ratio method yielded the lowest root mean square error (RMSE, 0.105) and mean absolute error (MAE, 0.088). Pairwise DeLong testing showed no statistically significant AUC difference among the three top-performing GGO-referenced methods. Conclusions In this single-center internal validation study, lesion-adaptive GGO-referenced methods showed more favorable overall pixel-level discrimination and lesion-level agreement than universal fixed thresholds or lesion-summary estimators. These rules should be considered developmental quantitative methods and require multicenter external validation across CT platforms and reconstruction protocols before routine clinical use.

title: Lung adenocarcinoma with rapid progression and fatal outcome through spread through air spaces: an autopsy case report.
abstract: Background Spread through air spaces (STAS), defined as tumor cell dissemination into alveolar spaces, is a prognostic factor for early-stage non-small cell lung cancer and is typically identified in surgical specimens from patients with early-stage disease. We describe a rare autopsy case of rapid progression with STAS in a patient with recurrent lung adenocarcinoma. Case description A 70-year-old man with stage IA lung adenocarcinoma previously treated with stereotactic radiotherapy and multiple comorbidities, including chronic heart failure due to the dilated phase of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, ventricular tachycardia treated with amiodarone, and diabetes mellitus, was admitted because of progressive dyspnea and respiratory failure. Computed tomography (CT) revealed bilateral ground-glass opacities with increased consolidation at the site of prior irradiation. Given the elevated liver attenuation on CT, amiodarone-induced pulmonary toxicity and pulmonary edema were initially suspected, the drug was discontinued, and diuretic therapy was intensified. Despite additional corticosteroid therapy and antibiotics for concurrent bacteremia, respiratory failure progressed and the patient died on hospital day 37. Autopsy revealed papillary adenocarcinoma with extensive STAS, characterized by tumor cell clusters floating within the airspaces in a micropapillary pattern, spreading bilaterally. Mucin staining revealed no abundant mucin in the cytoplasm, and thyroid transcription factor-1 was positive. No evidence of amiodarone-induced pneumonitis or significant pulmonary edema was observed. Conclusions To our knowledge, this is the first reported autopsy case of recurrent advanced lung adenocarcinoma with fatal respiratory failure in which extensive STAS was considered a major contributing factor. Clinicians should consider STAS as a potential mechanism of rapid deterioration in patients with known lung adenocarcinoma.

originalAbstract:
Background

Spread through air spaces (STAS), defined as tumor cell dissemination into alveolar spaces, is a prognostic factor for early-stage non-small cell lung cancer and is typically identified in surgical specimens from patients with early-stage disease. We describe a rare autopsy case of rapid progression with STAS in a patient with recurrent lung adenocarcinoma.

Case description

A 70-year-old man with stage IA lung adenocarcinoma previously treated with stereotactic radiotherapy and multiple comorbidities, including chronic heart failure due to the dilated phase of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, ventricular tachycardia treated with amiodarone, and diabetes mellitus, was admitted because of progressive dyspnea and respiratory failure. Computed tomography (CT) revealed bilateral ground-glass opacities with increased consolidation at the site of prior irradiation. Given the elevated liver attenuation on CT, amiodarone-induced pulmonary toxicity and pulmonary edema were initially suspected, the drug was discontinued, and diuretic therapy was intensified. Despite additional corticosteroid therapy and antibiotics for concurrent bacteremia, respiratory failure progressed and the patient died on hospital day 37. Autopsy revealed papillary adenocarcinoma with extensive STAS, characterized by tumor cell clusters floating within the airspaces in a micropapillary pattern, spreading bilaterally. Mucin staining revealed no abundant mucin in the cytoplasm, and thyroid transcription factor-1 was positive. No evidence of amiodarone-induced pneumonitis or significant pulmonary edema was observed.

Conclusions

To our knowledge, this is the first reported autopsy case of recurrent advanced lung adenocarcinoma with fatal respiratory failure in which extensive STAS was considered a major contributing factor. Clinicians should consider STAS as a potential mechanism of rapid deterioration in patients with known lung adenocarcinoma.

title: An integrated baseline CT model for predicting growth heterogeneity in solid lung cancer with transcriptomic annotation.
abstract: Background Solid nodular lung cancer exhibits significant heterogeneity in growth behavior, and the speed of growth is significantly correlated with prognosis. This study aimed to develop and validate an integrated baseline model for predicting growth heterogeneity in solid lung cancer and to provide exploratory transcriptomic annotation. Methods This study included 585 retrospectively collected surgically resected solid lung cancer nodules from March 2011 to December 2025, randomly divided into training and internal test cohorts at a 7:3 ratio. Forty-two nodules prospectively enrolled from January 2026 to June 2026 were used for prospective time validation. Fast and slow growth were defined by first-to-last volume doubling time (VDT), with a threshold of 400 days. Clinical, computer tomography (CT) morphological, intratumoral and peritumoral radiomics features were extracted from baseline CT. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) logistic regression was used for feature selection, and three score systems and seven predictive models were constructed. Whole transcriptome sequencing was performed in a quality-controlled subset of 54 lung adenocarcinoma nodules. Results The VDT of all enrolled nodules was 410.0 [interquartile range (IQR), 206.0-828.0] days, with a median follow-up interval of 173.0 (IQR, 80.0-481.0) days. The training, testing, and prospective time validation cohorts consisted of 409 (rapid vs. slow: 199 vs. 210), 176 (rapid vs. slow: 87 vs. 89), and 42 nodules (rapid vs. slow: 21 vs. 21), respectively. The Clinical-Intra-Peri model achieved the highest area under the curve (AUC) in the training and internal test cohorts, with AUCs of 0.754 and 0.770, respectively. Bootstrap internal validation yielded an optimism-corrected AUC of 0.750. In the prospective temporal validation cohort, the AUC was 0.825. Transcriptomic annotation showed that MYC targets V2 and unfolded protein response pathways, with leading-edge genes H2AX and MCM4, suggesting potential links between model-derived risk and growth-related transcriptomic activity. Conclusions The baseline Clinical-Intra-Peri CT model showed potential for predicting growth heterogeneity in solid lung cancer. Exploratory transcriptomic annotation suggested that model-defined risk was associated with growth-related transcriptional programs.

title: Dynamic Radiologic Severity Index is associated with antifungal treatment but does not independently predict initiation in pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia with post-chemotherapy pneumonia.
abstract: Background Invasive fungal pneumonia remains a diagnostic challenge in immunocompromised children with acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), as conventional microbiological tests have limited sensitivity. This retrospective study evaluated whether serial chest computed tomography (CT) scored with the Radiologic Severity Index (RSI) was associated with initiation of antifungal therapy in 87 children with ALL and chemotherapy-related pneumonia. Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted on 87 pediatric patients [median age 6.2 years, interquartile range (IQR) 3.5-8.0 years] diagnosed with ALL who developed pneumonia during chemotherapy between March 2016 and October 2024. Demographic data, medical history, and laboratory findings were collected for each patient. Chest CT images were assessed using the RSI, which quantifies affected lung volume and regional opacity (range 0-48). Clinical and radiologic characteristics of fungal and non-fungal pneumonia cases were compared using t-tests, Mann-Whitney U tests, Pearson's Chi-squared tests, or Fisher's exact tests. Additionally, binary logistic regression models were employed to examine the correlation between RSI and antifungal therapy initiation. Results No significant differences in baseline or peak RSI were observed between fungal and non-fungal groups, nor between antifungal-treated and untreated groups (all P>0.05). Routine laboratory parameters, including leukocyte, neutrophil, and lymphocyte counts, as well as serum albumin levels, did not differ between groups (all P>0.05). However, the antifungal-treated group demonstrated significantly higher change from baseline to peak Radiologic Severity Index (ΔRSI) (P=0.01) and RSI variation rate (P=0.02) compared to the untreated group. In multivariable logistic regression adjusted for potential confounders, neither ΔRSI [odds ratio (OR) =1.14, 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.94-1.37, P=0.18] nor RSI variation rate (OR =0.54, 95% CI: 0.15-1.98, P=0.36) emerged as an independent predictor of antifungal therapy initiation. Conclusions Dynamic RSI metrics (ΔRSI and RSI variation rate) are significantly elevated in pediatric ALL patients with chemotherapy-related pneumonia who receive antifungal therapy, whereas static RSI metrics and routine laboratory parameters are not. However, after adjusting for clinical confounders, dynamic RSI metrics do not independently predict antifungal treatment initiation. These findings suggest that serial CT monitoring and dynamic RSI assessment may reflect clinically meaningful disease progression, but current evidence does not support their use as standalone predictive tools for antifungal therapy decisions. Prospective studies with standardized imaging protocols are warranted to validate these exploratory results.

title: Persistent cerebrospinal fluid tumor cells during transient radiographic response in bilateral retinoblastoma with central nervous system involvement: a pediatric case report.
abstract: Background Central nervous system (CNS) involvement in retinoblastoma carries a poor prognosis, and the frequency and clinical meaning of discordance between structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cytology are not well defined. This report describes a compartment-specific mixed response and emphasizes the complementary roles of MRI and serial CSF assessment. Case description A 6-year-11-month-old boy presented after 6 months of progressive left proptosis, tearing, and conjunctival injection, without seizures or somnolence. Examination showed marked left proptosis and corneal opacity. MRI demonstrated bilateral ocular abnormalities, direct extension along the left optic nerve and chiasm, and a 29.3 mm × 25.8 mm intracranial lesion; malignant cells were present in CSF. Four cycles of vincristine, carboplatin, and etoposide reduced the intracranial lesion to 8.7 mm × 7.5 mm, but the left intraocular lesion did not clearly regress, optic nerve thickness increased from 4.9 mm after two cycles to 5.4 mm after four cycles, and CSF remained cytologically positive. Treatment was intensified for cycles 5-6 with cyclophosphamide-containing systemic chemotherapy and intrathecal methotrexate plus cytarabine. After six cycles, the intracranial lesion enlarged to 11.4 mm × 8.6 mm, optic nerve thickness increased to 6.7 mm, and CSF tumor cells persisted. Severe myelosuppression, infection, transfusion requirements, and family-related barriers prevented further treatment. The child died in March 2026, approximately 10 months after diagnosis. Germline testing prompted by bilateral disease identified a pathogenic RB1 c.772_776del (p.Asn258GlufsTer11) variant that was absent from parental blood. Conclusions The early reduction in measurable intracranial tumor burden did not represent CSF clearance and was followed by radiographic progression. In selected patients with CNS-involved retinoblastoma, MRI and CSF cytology provide complementary, non-interchangeable information; this single case supports integrated reassessment but does not establish a new response protocol.

title: Predictive value of novel inflammatory markers for post-infectious pulmonary embolism in children.
abstract: Background Pulmonary embolism (PE) is an increasingly recognized life-threatening condition in children, characterized by aberrant thrombo-inflammatory responses. New inflammatory markers such as systemic inflammation response index (SIRI), aggregate index of systemic inflammation (AISI), systemic immune-inflammation index (SII), neutrophil to lymphocyte ratio (NLR), monocyte to lymphocyte ratio (MLR), and platelet to lymphocyte ratio (PLR) are associated with the prediction and prognosis of PE. This study aimed to investigate the expression levels of biological markers such as D-dimer in acute PE of varying severity, and to discuss their correlations, thereby providing a reference for the early clinical identification of children with infection-associated acute PE. Methods A retrospective analysis was performed on data from 28 inpatients diagnosed with PE on imaging, including 24 with infection-related PE (post-infectious PE) and 4 with non-infectious PE (all with tumors), and 43 controls without PE on computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA) (control group), all of whom were admitted to the Children's Hospital of Chongqing Medical University from January 2010 to June 2024. The study aimed to compare the levels of novel inflammatory indicators between the groups and to evaluate their predictive value for diagnosing PE. Results There were 24 cases in the PE group, 9 men and 15 women, with a mean age of 94.42±43.76 months; 43 cases in the control group, 19 men and 24 women, with a mean age of 90.95±44.95 months. The differences in sex composition ratio and age between the two groups were not statistically significant (P>0.05). The values of NLR, MLR, SII, SIRI, and AISI in the PE group were higher than those in the control group (all P<0.05), and multifactorial logistic regression analysis revealed that patients with high levels of NLR, SIRI, and AISI had a higher risk of morbidity. The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves showed that the values of NLR [area under the curve (AUC): 0.794; 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.682 to 0.905], SIRI (AUC: 0.861; 95% CI: 0.772 to 0.951) and AISI (AUC: 0.859; 95% CI: 0.766 to 0.953), and AISI had a higher specificity, and the combination of the three had a higher sensitivity. Conclusions Elevated NLR, SIRI, and AISI levels were significantly associated with the presence of PE in children with infections, suggesting their utility as adjunctive biomarkers for the early identification of children with PE. NLR emerged as the most robust independent predictor. Given the cross-sectional design and limited sample size, the predictive value for disease severity or prognosis was not evaluated.

title: Diagnostic Performance and Clinical Outcomes of Intraoperative Neuromonitoring in Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis: A Comprehensive Analysis of 5,206 Patients.
abstract: Background Curve-specific risk factors for intraoperative neuromonitoring (IONM) alerts during surgery for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) remain unclear. Methods We identified 5,206 patients with AIS who underwent spinal fusion with multimodal IONM from a prospective database. Alerts were defined as ≥50% amplitude decrease in somatosensory evoked potentials (SSEPs) and/or transcranial motor evoked potentials (TcMEPs), or >10% SSEP latency increase. Demographics, radiographic parameters, surgical variables, triggering events, interventions, and outcomes were compared between the 252 patients with and 4,954 without an alert. Results IONM alerts occurred in 5% of patients. Alert rates varied by Lenke classification, with Type-4 curves demonstrating the highest risk (8%; relative risk [RR] = 1.61, 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.15 to 2.24) and Type 5 demonstrating the lowest risk (2%; RR = 0.45, 95% CI, 0.25 to 0.82). Patients with an alert had a larger mean preoperative major Cobb angle (66.7° ± 15.0° versus 56.1° ± 12.1°, p < 0.001) and more frequent use of Ponte osteotomies (79% versus 66%, p < 0.001). Multivariable analysis demonstrated the major Cobb angle to be the leading independent risk factor for alerts (p < 0.001). Hypotension was the leading triggering event (23%), and raising blood pressure was the most common intervention overall (52%). Neurologic deficits occurred in 4% of patients with an alert versus <1% of those without an alert (p < 0.001). Only 12 patients (<1%) experienced neurologic deficits, with 2 having permanent deficits. At 2-year follow-up, the major Cobb angle correction did not differ significantly between the groups with and without alerts, alert status did not independently affect correction (p = 0.058), and the groups achieved similar outcomes (73% versus 71% correction, respectively). Conclusions IONM alerts occurred in 5% of patients with AIS and were independently associated with a larger major Cobb angle. Fewer than 1% of patients sustained a permanent neurologic injury, and alerts did not appear to compromise 2-year correction. Level of evidence Prognostic Level III. abstract: Background Existing classifications for forearm deformity in multiple hereditary exostoses (MHE) have demonstrated low interrater reliability and limited clinical applicability. Our primary research question was whether a Delphi consensus process could generate a more reliable and clinically useful classification for longitudinal surveillance of MHE-related forearm deformities. Methods Fifteen pediatric hand surgeons from the Congenital Upper Limb Difference (CoULD) Study Group participated in 7 rounds of online Delphi surveys (June 2022 to September 2023). An investigator team facilitated the process with anonymized feedback. Round 1 identified key clinical and radiographic features. Subsequent rounds refined these features, determined categorical structure, and piloted the system with representative radiographs. Consensus was defined as ≥70% agreement. After final consensus, interrater reliability was tested by 4 independent surgeons who classified 101 radiographs from 67 patients with forearm MHE. Reliability was assessed with kappa and concordance coefficients and compared with the Masada, Gottschalk, and Jo classifications. Results The Delphi process identified radiographic predictors that included ulnar variance, the radial articular angle (RAA), radial head alignment, and osteochondroma size. Consensus favored a 3-tier classification: Type 1, mild; Type 2, moderate; and Type 3, severe. Closing consensus was achieved, with 93% agreement. Reliability testing showed moderate agreement on the first reading (kappa = 0.55), significantly higher than for the Masada (kappa = 0.21 [original classification], kappa = 0.35 [modified version]), Gottschalk (kappa = 0.43), and Jo (kappa = 0.43) classifications. After refinement that incorporated osteochondroma size and the radial head subtypes (3A, subluxation, and 3B, dislocation), agreement improved to substantial (kappa = 0.64) (p < 0.001), with high concordance (0.82). Conclusions The CoULD MHE Classification, developed through expert consensus, integrates validated radiographic predictors with defined thresholds. It demonstrated significantly improved reliability over prior systems and provides a practical framework for longitudinal monitoring of forearm deformities in patients with MHE. Level of evidence Diagnostic Level V. See Instructions for Authors for a complete description of levels of evidence.

title: Ability of Deep Learning to Predict Surgical Recommendations for Distal Radial Fractures: A Feasibility Study.
abstract: Background Distal radial fractures (DRFs) are extremely common, and decisions regarding operative intervention rely on clinical judgment and radiographic parameters at and after injury. Understanding whether a recommendation will be made for operative versus nonoperative management in an initial point-of-care setting can assist in patient counseling and reinforce timely follow-up with general orthopaedic or hand specialists. This study investigated the feasibility of using artificial intelligence (AI) to predict whether a fellowship-trained hand surgeon would recommend operative intervention using pre-reduction radiographs and clinical and demographic data. Methods A convolutional neural network (CNN) model was trained on pre-reduction injury radiographs, and its outputs were combined with clinical and demographic data in a random forest (RF) model. The final model was evaluated on a hold-out test data set. To enhance interpretability, gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM) heatmaps and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) were employed to identify image regions and clinical features contributing to model predictions. Results Of 1,040 included patients, 884 were used for training and 156 for testing model performance. On the test data set, the combined model achieved an accuracy of 87.14%, sensitivity of 97%, specificity of 73%, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.96, and Brier score of 0.10. Grad-CAM visualizations indicated that the CNN focused on clinically relevant features, such as fracture displacement, and SHAP analysis of the RF model highlighted age and lateral wrist radiographs as key contributors to predictions. Conclusions This pilot study demonstrates the feasibility of using AI to predict the recommendations of a group of fellowship-trained hand surgeons at 1 institution regarding operative versus nonoperative treatment for a DRF on the basis of pre-reduction injury radiographs and clinical and demographic data. Future work will focus on external validation, expanding data sets, and incorporating additional imaging features to optimize performance and generalizability. Level of evidence Prognostic Level III . See Instructions for Authors for a complete description of levels of evidence.

title: Validation of the Bone-RADS (Bone Reporting and Data System) Score for Predicting Risk of Malignancy.
abstract: Background Bone-RADS (Bone Reporting and Data System) is a consensus guideline by the American College of Radiology to assist in the risk stratification of lytic bone lesions. A score is calculated using 5 radiographic factors and a history of primary malignancy. The purpose of this study was to externally validate the Bone-RADS scoring system. Methods This retrospective review examined radiographs from January 1, 2021, to December 31, 2021. Radiographs were identified via a keyword search for "lucent," "osteolytic," or "lytic" in extremity radiograph reports. All radiographs were initially read by a musculoskeletal radiologist. Radiographs of skeletally immature patients, lesions in a bone other than a long bone, primary soft-tissue masses, and negative/normal radiographs were excluded. Radiographs were independently scored on the basis of the Bone-RADS system by 4 reviewers. In the absence of a biopsy, a lesion was considered benign if it remained stable for 2 years on radiographs. Scores were correlated with final diagnoses to calculate the rates of malignancy and malignant transformation. Results Of 1,108 screened radiographs, 423 were eligible. The mean age of the patients was 62 years and 49% were male. A higher Bone-RADS score was associated with a malignant diagnosis (p < 0.001), with an odds ratio of 9.7 (95% confidence interval [CI], 6.2 to 14.9) per 1-unit increase in the score. A higher margin score (p < 0.001), endosteal erosion (p < 0.001), a pathologic fracture (p < 0.001), and a soft-tissue mass (p = 0.02) were associated with increased risk of malignancy. The mean inter-rater agreement (weighted kappa) was 0.52, the inter-rater mean absolute deviation (MAD) was 0.37, and the intra-rater MAD was 0.27. Sensitivity was 97.1% (CI, 94.4% to 98.5%), specificity was 67.4% (CI, 59.3% to 74.5%), positive predictive value was 85.2% (CI, 80.9% to 88.7%), and negative predictive value was 92.4% (CI, 85.7% to 96.1%). Conclusions The Bone-RADS scoring system demonstrated moderate diagnostic performance for malignancy risk stratification of lytic bone lesions, with high sensitivity and reproducible binary classification of possibly benign versus malignant. Although inter-rater agreement for the 4-tier score was only moderate, clinically relevant benign-versus-malignant categorization demonstrated higher inter- and intra-rater agreement. These findings support Bone-RADS as a practical triage framework based on musculoskeletal imaging of lytic bone lesions. Level of evidence Diagnostic Level III. title: Extra-Articular Malunions and Nonunions of the Scapular Body and Neck: A Comparison of Functional Outcomes Before and After Reconstruction.
abstract: Background Malunions and nonunions of scapular neck and body fractures can cause considerable pain and disability. This study reports outcomes regarding functional measures, range of motion, and strength before and after reconstruction. Methods This retrospective case series at a Level-1 trauma center between 2003 and 2024 identified 50 consecutive patients (mean age, 50.3 years; 82% male; 80% White) with symptomatic malunion or nonunion of a scapular neck and/or body fracture who were referred to a single surgeon. Medial-lateral displacement and angular deformity were corrected through surgical reconstruction and malunion osteotomy. The Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand (DASH) score, range of motion, strength, and postoperative procedures requiring a return to the operating room were recorded. Results Fifty patients were included in the study; 5 patients were lost to follow-up before 12 months, leaving 45 patients (40 with malunion and 5 with nonunion) with >1-year outcomes. Eleven patients underwent reconstruction between 6 weeks and 3 months after injury because of the severity of the injury, their symptoms, and/or the necessity of an osteotomy. The median time from injury to reconstruction was 10 months (interquartile range [IQR] width, 16 months), and the median follow-up was 28.9 months (IQR width, 23.2 months). All patients achieved radiographic evidence of union. No intraoperative complications occurred. There was a mean 30.7-point improvement between the preoperative and final postoperative DASH scores (p < 0.001). The mean postoperative DASH score was 14.1 in patients who underwent reconstruction between 6 weeks and 3 months and was 23.2 in those who underwent reconstruction after 3 months. Forward flexion and abduction demonstrated significant increases in both range of motion and strength from preoperatively to postoperatively. External rotation range of motion and strength showed no significant increases. Subsequent procedures were performed in 12 patients: 8 patients underwent symptomatic implant removal (1 also underwent concurrent manipulation under anesthesia), 1 patient underwent open reduction and internal fixation for a new fracture, 2 patients underwent implant revision (1 also underwent concurrent manipulation under anesthesia), and 1 patient underwent manipulation under anesthesia for shoulder contracture. Conclusions Extra-articular scapular malunions and nonunions can be associated with considerable pain and disability. Deformity correction improved range of motion and strength and reduced disability in this cohort. A principled reconstruction can be successful in addressing the sequelae of displaced scapular fractures. Level of evidence Therapeutic Level IV. title: Intraoperative recognition of low-grade appendiceal mucinous neoplasm masquerading as a right ovarian tumor: a case report
abstract: Abstract Background Low-grade appendiceal mucinous neoplasm (LAMN) is a mucin-producing epithelial tumor arising from the appendix. When the appendix is displaced into the pelvis and becomes cystically enlarged, LAMN may mimic a right ovarian mucinous tumor. Because rupture of LAMN may cause mucin spillage and pseudomyxoma peritonei, accurate intraoperative recognition and careful surgical handling are important. Case presentation: A 75-year-old Japanese woman was referred to our department with a right adnexal mass suspected to be an ovarian tumor. Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging revealed an approximately 7-cm cystic mass in the right adnexal region, and a right ovarian mucinous tumor was suspected preoperatively. Serum carcinoembryonic antigen was mildly elevated, whereas carbohydrate antigen 19 − 9 and cancer antigen 125 were not markedly elevated. Laparoscopic surgery was performed under the preoperative diagnosis of a right ovarian tumor. Intraoperatively, the uterus and bilateral adnexa were grossly normal. Instead, a cystic mass was identified near the right adnexal region and was continuous with the appendix and ileocecal region. The lesion was carefully resected without intraoperative rupture or mucin spillage. Intraoperative frozen section analysis showed no evidence of malignancy, and ascites cytology was negative. Histopathological examination revealed LAMN with a negative surgical margin. Immunohistochemical findings were consistent with an appendiceal origin and supported the diagnosis of LAMN. Postoperative computed tomography showed no evidence of residual disease or pseudomyxoma peritonei. Conclusion LAMN can mimic a right ovarian tumor. In right-sided mucinous adnexal masses, appendiceal origin should be considered, and rupture-free complete resection is essential to prevent pseudomyxoma peritonei.

title: Graph-Aware Medical Image Intelligence: A Comparative Study of CNNs, GNNs, and Multimodal LLMs for Acute Lymphoblastic Leukaemia Subtyping
abstract: Abstract The correct determination of the cell type of an acute leukaemia (ALL) is essential, since therapy depends on the morphological variations that can be seen in blood smear images. Manual microscopy is still a time-consuming, labor-intensive method and the results of the diagnosis often differ from one observer to another, which is the reason for the need of reliable automatic diagnostic models. This study compares and evaluates three deep learning paradigms - Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), and multimodal Large Language Models (LLMs) - for the classification of four ALL subtypes from the Multi Cancer Dataset (4000 images). The CNN models used were trained with the same preprocessing steps, including resizing, normalization and augmentation, to promote generalization to other tasks. Based on the spatially segmented nuclei and morphological features, four GNN models were designed to capture inter-cell relationships that are not captured by pixel-based architectures. Furthermore, a multimodal model ViT–BERT and its fine-tuned version were also used to incorporate visual embeddings and text domain knowledge. The tuned ViT–BERT model achieved F1 = 0.99, matching the top CNN baselines (DenseNet121, MobileNetV2 at F1 = 0.98) and outperforming InceptionV3 and ResNet50. The graph-based reasoning models were found to perform competitively on the subtypes with unique spatial arrangement of cells, showing the importance of reasoning on graphs. Interpretability was addressed through Grad-CAM for CNN and multimodal models, and GNN Explainer for graph architectures, being transparent in model decisions. The results suggest that the pixel-level, graph-level, and multimodal representations are effective in enhancing accuracy and interpretability, which helps to build more reliable diagnostic systems for ALL.

title: Design of the Precision Medicine for more Oxygen Interstitial Lung Disease (P4O2-ILD) study: a Dutch prospective observational cohort study to identify risk factors and biomarkers for progressive fibrotic interstitial lung diseases
abstract: Abstract Background: Pulmonary fibrosis is a common end-stage manifestation of a wide range of interstitial lung diseases (ILDs). Progressive pulmonary fibrosis (PPF) is currently defined by longitudinal deterioration in symptoms, lung function, and/or radiological findings, often indicating that substantial and irreversible lung damage has already occurred. Consequently, the optimal timing of therapeutic intervention remains a matter of ongoing debate, highlighting the need for earlier identification of patients at risk of developing a progressive fibrotic phenotype. The P4O2 ILD study aims to identify risk factors and biomarkers associated with the development of PPF and clinically significant ILD. Methods: The P4O2 ILD study is a prospective observational cohort study that will enroll 450 participants from hospitals across the Netherlands. Three arms of participants will be included: (1) patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis or fibrotic ILD in the context of familial pulmonary fibrosis carrying pathogenic variants in established pulmonary fibrosis-associated genes (n = 150); (2) patients with other fibrotic ILDs, including idiopathic fibrotic bronchiolocentric interstitial pneumonia, fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis, idiopathic fibrotic nonspecific interstitial pneumonia, connective tissue disease-associated ILD, and unclassifiable ILD (n = 150); and (3) individuals with interstitial lung abnormalities (ILA) (n = 150). Participants will undergo serial assessments over a five-year follow-up period, comprising eight study visits. Evaluations include blood sampling for peripheral blood mononuclear cells and plasma analyses, pulmonary function testing, chest computed tomography, exposome and multi-omics profiling, patient-reported outcome measures, and lower airway sampling using the particles in exhaled air technique. A subgroup of participants will additionally undergo bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage. Discussion: To identify biomarkers associated with the onset and progression of pulmonary fibrosis, the study will compare ILD subtypes that differ in their for and the rate and timing of fibrotic progression. Findings will be interpreted in the context of data obtained from a population-based healthy cohort and a cohort at increased risk of lung disease (P4O2-PARASOL). This comprehensive approach is expected to facilitate earlier detection of disease progression, improve patient stratification, guide treatment strategies, and support prevention and monitoring efforts in individuals with ILA. Trial Registration: This prospective observational cohort study is registered on 23th of September 2024 in the International Clinical Trial Registry, www.clinicaltrials.gov; IDNCT06644144. Trial Status: Recruitment began on 28-11-2024 and is ongoing. As of 14-8-2026, 37 of the planned 450 participants have been enrolled. If recruitment targets are not reached within three years, the inclusion period will be extended until the target sample size is achieved.

title: Pleomorphic Adenoma of the Upper Lip: A Case Report with Histopathological and Clinical Correlation
abstract: Abstract Background Pleomorphic adenoma (PA), often called benign mixed tumour is the most common salivary gland neoplasm. Majority of the tumours occur in major salivary glands from while only 10% occurs in minor salivary glands. Cases of PA in the oral cavity have been mainly reported in palate and respectively in the upper lip. Case presentation In this case report, we describe a case of pleomorphic adenoma with a rare clinical feature. A 49-year-old female reported to the dental hospital with a complain of slowly developing reddish-yellow coloured painless swelling in the left upper labial vestibule since 5 years. Temporary pain and temperature sensitivity have also been reported. Radiographically, there is no evidence of any radiolucency. Hence, Lipoma, mucocele, minor salivary gland tumour was considered as the differential diagnosis as these lesions are also reported in the upper lip, and they can show these clinical features. An excisional biopsy was taken. It shows a biphasic proliferation of epithelial cells and myoepithelial cells in cords and well-defined aggregates in a mixed myxoid/chondroid stroma. It shows a well-circumscribed lesion features typical for PA of the upper lip. The post-operative period was uneventful, and on 3-month follow-up, no recurrence was noted. Conclusions Pleomorphic adenoma of the upper lip is an uncommon benign neoplasm that should be included in the differential diagnosis of persistent mucosal swellings. This case highlights the importance of histopathological confirmation to ensure optimal patient outcomes.

title: BioPretext: A Multimodal Self-Supervised Learning Framework for Orthopedic Feature Extraction via Cross-Modal Signal Alignment and Dynamic Fusion
abstract: Abstract We propose BioPretext, a multimodal self-supervised learning (SSL) framework that unifies geometric and non-geometric biological signals for orthopedic feature extraction. Unlike conventional approaches that process imaging data independently, BioPretext exploits interactions between structural and functional modalities through cross-modal pretext tasks. The framework employs a dual-branch transformer architecture, where a vision transformer encodes geometric data (e.g., radiographs) and a temporal transformer processes sequential biological signals (e.g., EKG). Both representations are projected into a shared latent space via cross-attention. To improve robustness, two contrastive pretext tasks—signal inversion and time-window masking—are introduced, enabling recovery of corrupted or missing biological signals using geometric context. Extracted features are then integrated through a gated attention mechanism that adaptively weights modality contributions according to task relevance. The framework can replace conventional feature extraction modules in orthopedic AI systems and be readily applied to downstream tasks such as joint kinematics prediction and lesion segmentation. Key innovations include cross-modal SSL optimization, temporal-spatial alignment, and patient-specific dynamic fusion. Implemented with Swin Transformer and Performer backbones, BioPretext is pretrained on unlabeled multimodal datasets and subsequently fine-tuned for orthopedic applications. Experimental results demonstrate superior performance over unimodal SSL approaches, particularly in tasks involving complex interactions between biological and structural data, such as gait analysis and osteoarthritis grading. These findings highlight the potential of BioPretext as a scalable and generalizable framework for multimodal representation learning in orthopedics.

title: Hearing impairment is associated with impaired glymphatic function in middle- and older-aged adults: evidence from DTI-ALPS imaging
abstract: Abstract Hearing impairment is a common age-related sensory disorder and has been increasingly linked to central nervous system changes beyond peripheral auditory dysfunction. This study aimed to investigate the relationship between hearing impairment and glymphatic system function using the diffusion tensor imaging along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS) index, and to explore its potential as an imaging biomarker in middle- and older-aged adults. A total of 131 participants aged 45–80 years were enrolled, including 71 individuals with normal hearing and 60 with hearing impairment defined by pure-tone average thresholds ≥ 25 dB HL. All participants underwent brain MRI with diffusion tensor imaging, and glymphatic function was evaluated using the DTI-ALPS index. Cognitive function was assessed using the Mini-Mental State Examination and Montreal Cognitive Assessment. Associations between pure-tone average and DTI-ALPS indices were examined using Spearman correlation analysis. Logistic regression models were applied to identify independent factors associated with hearing impairment, and receiver operating characteristic analysis was used to evaluate diagnostic performance. Participants with hearing impairment were older, more frequently male, and exhibited lower MoCA scores compared with controls. Global and regional DTI-ALPS indices were significantly reduced in the hearing impairment group and were inversely correlated with hearing thresholds. In multivariate analysis, both older age and lower DTI-ALPS index remained independently associated with hearing impairment. The combined model incorporating age and DTI-ALPS achieved the best discriminative performance. These findings suggest that hearing impairment is independently associated with reduced glymphatic system function, and that the DTI-ALPS index, particularly when combined with age, may serve as a promising imaging biomarker for age-related hearing decline.

title: QFR-guided versus IVUS-guided with QFR confirmation for drug-coated balloon treatment of non-complex coronary lesions: a single-centre pilot randomised trial
abstract: Abstract Background: Drug-coated balloon (DCB) angioplasty for the treatment of coronary artery lesions relies on adequate lesion pre-treatment, yet the optimal strategy for intraoperative imaging guidance remains unclear. This randomized controlled pilot trial aims to evaluate the feasibility of a strategy combining quantitative flow ratio (QFR) guidance with intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) guidance and QFR validation (IVUS+QFR) in the treatment of non-complex coronary artery lesions with DCB, and to provide estimates of the effect size for follow-up studies. Methods: This study was a prospective, single-center, open-label randomized controlled pilot trial, enrolling a total of 78 patients (82 vessels; 4 patients contributed 2 vessels each). Participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to the QFR-guided group (43 vessels) or the IVUS+QFR-guided group (39 vessels). The primary endpoint was immediate post-procedural functional success, defined as a post-PCI QFR ≥ 0.90 assessed offline by the core laboratory. The primary effect measure was the absolute risk difference (RD) and its 95% confidence interval(calculated using a patient-level clustered bootstrap method). Results: All 78 patients completed the assigned protocol, and the primary endpoint data of 82 vessels were fully obtained (100% feasibility). The rate of functional success was 79.1% (34/43) in the QFR-guided group and 84.6% (33/39) in the IVUS+QFR-guided group. The relative difference (RD) between the two groups was −5.5 percentage points (95% CI: −21.3 to 11.7). The odds ratio (OR) adjusted for covariates was 0.58 (95% CI: 0.18–1.85; P = 0.357). The confidence interval is too wide to draw a definitive conclusion regarding the superiority or inferiority of strategy , which is consistent with the exploratory nature of a pilot trial. Conclusions: Both QFR-guided and IVUS+QFR-guided strategies demonstrated complete procedural feasibility in DCB treatment. The effect size estimates and confidence interval precision provided by this study may serve as important references for sample size calculation in future confirmatory trials. Trial registration: Trial registration: Chinese Clinical Trial Registry ChiCTR2400084789 (registered on 24 May 2024; Retrospectively registered).

title: CT-Based Habitat Radiomics and Deep Learning for Predicting Early Response and Survival in Unresectable Hepatocellular Carcinoma Treated with Hepatic Arterial Infusion Chemotherapy plus Lenvatinib and Programmed Death Receptor-1 Inhibitors
abstract: Abstract Background The marked intratumoral heterogeneity of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) leads to substantial variability in treatment response among patients receiving HAIC-FOLFOX combined with lenvatinib and PD-1 inhibitors. This study aimed to develop a multidimensional fusion model integrating habitat radiomics, 2.5D deep learning features, and clinical indicators to predict early objective response and progression-free survival in these patients. Methods This dual-center retrospective study enrolled 240 patients with unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma treated with HAIC-FOLFOX combined with lenvatinib and PD-1 inhibitors. Patients from Center 1 were randomly assigned in a 7:3 ratio to a training cohort (n = 112) and an internal validation cohort (n = 49), while 79 patients from Center 2 constituted the independent external testing cohort. Habitat imaging was employed to decompose the tumor into phenotypically distinct subregions via K-means clustering. Radiomics features were then extracted from the whole-tumor region and each habitat subregion on pretreatment contrast-enhanced CT images. Four 2.5D convolutional neural networks were trained for deep feature extraction. Machine learning models, including a combined model constructed through feature-level and decision-level fusion, were evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), calibration curves, and decision curve analysis. SHapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) analysis was performed for model interpretability. Results The combined model achieved AUCs of 0.911 (95% CI: 0.855–0.967), 0.883 (95% CI: 0.780–0.987), and 0.871 (95% CI: 0.792–0.949) in the training, internal validation, and external testing cohorts, respectively. Calibration curves demonstrated favorable agreement between predicted and observed outcomes. Decision curve analysis confirmed higher net clinical benefit for the combined model. DeLong's test showed the combined model significantly outperformed all other models in the external testing cohort (all P < 0.05). The model-derived risk stratification effectively discriminated progression-free survival across all three cohorts (all log-rank P < 0.001). Conclusion The combined model offers a noninvasive tool for pretreatment prediction of both early objective response and progression-free survival in patients with unresectable HCC undergoing HAIC combined with lenvatinib and PD-1 inhibitors, potentially informing individualized treatment decisions.

title: SFCT-Net: A Wavelet-Based Spatial-Frequency Signal Reconstruction Framework for Robust Medical Image Segmentation
abstract: Abstract Medical ultrasound and dermoscopic images can be interpreted as corrupted signals in both spatial and frequency domains, presenting profound challenges for automated segmentation due to intrinsic sensor degradations such as acoustic speckle noise and low-frequency contrast attenuation. In conventional automated segmentation, treating this task purely as a spatial-domain pixel classification problem often relying on bilinear interpolation or transposed convolutions for decoding inevitably acts as a suboptimal low-pass filter. This spatial manipulation triggers severe frequency aliasing, severely degrading fragile high-frequency anatomical boundaries during the signal reconstruction process. To address this limitation, we redefine medical image segmentation as a spatial-frequency signal reconstruction problem and propose a robust wavelet-domain framework, SFCT-Net. To effectively capture features without sequential degradation, we deploy synchronized convolutional and self-attention streams, introducing an Asymmetric Cross-Interaction Module (ACIM) to dynamically calibrate and align these heterogeneous semantics. Crucially, as the primary signal reconstruction operator, we introduce the Wavelet-Driven Reconstruction Module (WRM). By seamlessly embedding the 2D Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT), WRM explicitly applies frequency decoupling, orthogonally isolating low-frequency semantic components from high-frequency edge contours. This paradigm executes targeted noise suppression and maintains strong structural consistency entirely within the frequency domain.Extensive evaluations on ten public medical image datasets indicate that the proposed framework consistently achieves competitive segmentation performance with improved boundary preservation and robust generalization across multiple imaging modalities.

title: Biopsies from Normal-Appearing Mucosa in Pediatric Upper GI Endoscopy: What Do They Tell Us?
abstract: Abstract Purpose: Histopathological abnormalities may be detected despite normal endoscopic findings in pediatric upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy. However, the clinical value of routine biopsies from macroscopically normal mucosa remains uncertain. We aimed to evaluate the impact of such biopsies on diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up. Methods: We conducted a retrospective study of children undergoing upper GI endoscopy at a tertiary care center over a one-year period. Biopsies obtained from macroscopically normal esophageal, gastric, and duodenal mucosa were analyzed. Biopsy findings were assessed for their impact on clinical management, defined as any change in treatment or follow-up. Results were evaluated according to both the number of affected patients and the total number of biopsy specimens. Results: A total of 802 endoscopies were included. Biopsies from normal-appearing mucosa were obtained in 577 patients (71.9%), yielding 2,055 biopsy specimens. Histopathological findings altered clinical management in 60 patients (10.4%). At the biopsy level, 116 specimens (5.6%) revealed clinically relevant findings, whereas 542 (26.4%) showed inflammatory changes without clinical impact and 1,397 (68.0%) were histologically normal. Most management-changing findings were related to Helicobacter pylori infection (26/60). Clinical impact varied according to presenting symptoms and biopsy site. Conclusions: Routine biopsy of macroscopically normal mucosa during pediatric upper GI endoscopy rarely influences clinical management. A selective biopsy strategy guided by presenting symptoms, clinical suspicion, and established guideline recommendations may optimize diagnostic yield while reducing unnecessary procedures.

title: Preoperative Prediction of Vascular Invasion in Breast Cancer Based on Habitat-Based Radiomics Integrating Intratumoral and Multidimensional Peritumoral Features: A Multicenter DCE-MRI Study
abstract: Abstract Background: Lymphatic vessel invasion (LVI) is widely recognized as an indicator of breast cancer aggressiveness and metastatic potential; however, the lack of non-invasive tools capable of capturing intratumoral and peritumoral heterogeneity continues to pose challenges for reliable preoperative prediction. Purpose: The aim of this study is to develop and rigorously validate a multimodal fusion model that integrates traditional radiomics, image features derived from habitat-based imaging, and clinical risk factors to enable non-invasive preoperative prediction of lymphatic vessel invasion (LVI) in breast cancer. Method: This retrospective study included 742 patients from two independent centers. Data from Center 1 (n = 628) were randomly split in a 7:3 ratio into a training set (n = 439) and an internal validation set (n = 189); Center 2 (n = 114) served as an independent external validation set. A comprehensive radiomic analysis was performed on DCE-MRI data, covering the intratumoral region and peritumoral expansion at five increasing distances (1, 3, 5, 7, and 10 mm). Tumor functional subregions (habitats) were identified using K-means clustering. The performance of nine machine learning algorithms was compared, and the optimal ExtraTrees habitat features were fused with independent clinical predictors (menopausal status and sentinel lymph node status) to construct the final combined model. Discrimination ability was assessed using AUC, accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity, while calibration and clinical utility were evaluated through calibration curve and decision curve analyses. Results: In the comparison of tumor-peripheral distances, the 7-mm combined with AdaBoost model demonstrated relatively good generalization ability (AUC of 0.674 in the external validation set), but the differences among the various distances were not statistically significant. Multivariate analysis revealed that menopausal status and sentinel lymph node status were independent predictors of LVI. The multimodal fusion model achieved the most balanced overall performance, with an AUC of 0.740 (95% CI: 0.646–0.834) in the independent external validation set, a precision of 72.8%, and a sensitivity as high as 71.2%. Although the AUC of the clinical-only model was slightly higher (0.713), the fusion model demonstrated significantly superior sensitivity (71.2% vs. 64.4%). The model showed good calibration, and ROC curve analysis confirmed that it provided clinical net benefit within a threshold probability range of 0.2–0.6. Conclusion: DCE-MRI-based in-tumor and peritumoral microenvironment omics analysis, combined with readily available clinical variables, offers a promising non-invasive approach for preoperative risk stratification of lymphatic vessel invasion (LVI) in breast cancer. This multimodal framework has undergone cross-device external validation and is expected to support personalized treatment decisions for breast cancer.

title: A case report of vulvar teratoma
abstract: Abstract Background Teratomas composed of tissues derived from all three germ layers are germ cell tumors originating from totipotent stem cells. While gonadal teratomas are common, extragonadal teratomas account for approximately 15% of all cases, with vulvar localization being exceptionally rare. To date, only a limited number of vulvar teratoma cases have been reported in the international literature. Case: A 19-year-old female presented with a vulvar mass first noted at birth that had progressively enlarged with age. Over the preceding year, the patient experienced intermittent inflammation and recurrent ulceration secondary to friction, accompanied by mild dysuria. Physical examination revealed a pedunculated mass measuring 5 × 4 cm situated between the clitoris and urethral meatus, together with a 2 × 2 cm urethral caruncle. Multimodal imaging including ultrasonography, computed tomography, and magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a mixed-echogenicity exophytic mass containing mesenteric and bowel-like structures with a prominent vascular pedicle extending toward the urethra and bladder trigone. The preoperative differential diagnosis included external parasitic twin (fetus in fetu) versus vulvar teratoma. The patient underwent complete surgical excision of the vulvar mass and the urethral caruncle under general anesthesia. Histopathological examination confirmed the diagnosis of a mature teratoma. Immunohistochemical analysis revealed CK8/18 (+), CK20 (+), CDX-2 (+), Vimentin (+), and a Ki-67 proliferation index of less than 10%. The postoperative course was uneventful. At one-month follow-up, the wound had healed completely with restoration of normal vulvar anatomy and preserved physiological function. Conclusion Mature teratoma of the vulva is a rare extragonadal neoplasm that may be misdiagnosed on imaging as a parasitic twin owing to overlapping radiological features. Complete surgical excision remains the treatment of choice and is associated with favorable outcomes. Heightened clinical awareness and correlation of imaging findings with histopathological evaluation are essential to establish an accurate diagnosis and guide appropriate management in such rare cases.

Case: A 19-year-old female presented with a vulvar mass first noted at birth that had progressively enlarged with age. Over the preceding year, the patient experienced intermittent inflammation and recurrent ulceration secondary to friction, accompanied by mild dysuria. Physical examination revealed a pedunculated mass measuring 5 × 4 cm situated between the clitoris and urethral meatus, together with a 2 × 2 cm urethral caruncle. Multimodal imaging including ultrasonography, computed tomography, and magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a mixed-echogenicity exophytic mass containing mesenteric and bowel-like structures with a prominent vascular pedicle extending toward the urethra and bladder trigone. The preoperative differential diagnosis included external parasitic twin (fetus in fetu) versus vulvar teratoma. The patient underwent complete surgical excision of the vulvar mass and the urethral caruncle under general anesthesia. Histopathological examination confirmed the diagnosis of a mature teratoma. Immunohistochemical analysis revealed CK8/18 (+), CK20 (+), CDX-2 (+), Vimentin (+), and a Ki-67 proliferation index of less than 10%. The postoperative course was uneventful. At one-month follow-up, the wound had healed completely with restoration of normal vulvar anatomy and preserved physiological function. Conclusion Mature teratoma of the vulva is a rare extragonadal neoplasm that may be misdiagnosed on imaging as a parasitic twin owing to overlapping radiological features. Complete surgical excision remains the treatment of choice and is associated with favorable outcomes. Heightened clinical awareness and correlation of imaging findings with histopathological evaluation are essential to establish an accurate diagnosis and guide appropriate management in such rare cases.

title: Pyogenic Liver Abscess Following ERCP and Biliary Stenting: A Case Series of Two Patients and Clinical Implications
abstract: Abstract Introduction: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is a critical diagnostic and therapeutic modality for choledocholithiasis, acute cholangitis, and obstructive jaundice. Although pyogenic liver abscess is a rare complication following ERCP, it carries significant clinical implications. We present two cases of pyogenic liver abscess developing after ERCP and biliary stent-related procedures in patients with choledocholithiasis. Case Presentation: Case 1 involved a 42-year-old female who developed a liver abscess in segment 4 following laparoscopic cholecystectomy, common bile duct exploration, intraoperative ERCP with stent placement, primary closure of the common bile duct, and drainage of a segment 4 hepatic cyst. The abscess manifested after stent removal and balloon sweeping of the bile duct, presenting with right upper quadrant pain, chills, and fever up to 39°C. Computed tomography (CT) confirmed a liver abscess in segment 4. Case 2 involved a 62-year-old male who underwent ERCP with sphincterotomy, basket stone extraction, and biliary stent placement for choledocholithiasis with obstructive jaundice. On postoperative day 6, he developed right upper quadrant pain, chills, and fever up to 39°C. CT revealed a new 32 mm × 26 mm abscess in the right hepatic lobe, with markedly elevated procalcitonin (63.7 ng/mL) and renal dysfunction. Both patients improved after percutaneous drainage, and Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae were isolated from abscess cultures in both cases. Conclusion: Although rare, pyogenic liver abscess should be considered in patients with biliary infection, stent placement or removal, sphincterotomy, complex biliary surgery, or pre-existing hepatic cystic lesions following ERCP. Early imaging evaluation with ultrasonography or contrast-enhanced CT is warranted when postoperative abdominal pain, chills, high fever, elevated inflammatory markers, or cholestasis abnormalities occur. Image-guided percutaneous drainage, combined with appropriate antimicrobial therapy, serves as an effective minimally invasive intervention for source control.

title: Acute coma with severe infection events: a population-based retrospective cohort study
abstract: Abstract Background Previous studies shown that acute coma is a very common public health issuer in global. However, the prevalence and high risk of death in acute coma with severe infection events(SIE) remains understudied. We aimed to investigate whether acute coma with high risk of death is related to SIE so that to improve its outcome. Metholds A retrospective study of adult acute coma patients with or without SIE is conducted from a teaching hospital sites in China. The patients who were underwent a systemic (I.e, brain lungs and abdomen) CT screening before ICU and confirmed wiith or without SIE is included in this study. The primary outcome is the prevalence and high risk of death from acute coma with SIE. Logistic or Cox proportional Hazard models with cubic sening. Results: From January 1, 2018, to Jamuary 1, 2023. A total of 1180 patients with acute coma were admitted to the ICU. We found that 839(70.4%) patients had SIE and 349(29.6%) did not. Of these, 64.3% were male, with a mean age of 66.8 years (SD, 16.3). Initial median Glasgow Coma Scales (GCS) score was 6.0 (IQR 3 to 8). In the ICU stay, 69.3% underwent invasive mechanical ventilation due to acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). Community- acquired pneumonia (82.1%, 969/1180) was the most common infection. There was significant differences in the potential risk factors for coma with SIE or without SIE. Adjusted odds ratio [aOR] achieved 6.9 (95% confidence intervals[CI] 4.30-7.48) for acute coma with SIE, 5.3(4,25-5.82) for extended cytokine storm duration, 3.5 (95% CI, 2.82- 5.17) for elevated SOFA scores, and 3.0(95%CI,2.18 - 4.83 ) for elevated cytokine levels. The aOR of coma with SIE was the highest as compared with the other risk factors. At the 28 days follow-up, survival rate was significantly lower among with SIE than without SIE ( HR for death, 3.1; p,0.001) and most died in the ICU. Conclusions: Highly prevalent acute coma with high risk of death is associated with SIE, supporting that acute coma should used an early systemic CT screening to identify SIE, and facilitate early treatment to improve outcomes.

title: Longitudinal CT-Based Assessment of Early Bone–Implant Interface Changes after 3D-Printed Titanium Limb-Salvage Reconstruction: A Finite Element and Radiomics Proof-of-Concept Study
abstract: Abstract Background Early assessment of bone–implant interface integration after 3D-printed titanium reconstruction remains challenging. This study aimed to explore the feasibility of a longitudinal CT-based framework integrating finite element analysis and radiomics for postoperative assessment of early interface changes after limb-salvage reconstruction. Methods A patient who underwent bone tumor resection followed by reconstruction with a patient-specific 3D-printed titanium prosthesis was retrospectively included. Serial thin-slice CT scans obtained at 1, 2, 3, and 4 months postoperatively were used for three-dimensional reconstruction, longitudinal rigid registration, finite element analysis under representative loading conditions, and CT radiomic feature extraction. Biomechanical indicators and radiomic features were analyzed descriptively across follow-up time points. Results Longitudinal finite element analysis showed a gradual decrease in total deformation, implant von Mises stress, and talar surface peak equivalent stress across the early postoperative period. CT radiomic analysis showed increasing first-order mean values, decreasing GLDM dependence non-uniformity, and increasing GLCM inverse variance. Exploratory correlation analysis suggested concordant temporal changes between selected biomechanical indicators and radiomic features. Conclusions This proof-of-concept study demonstrates the feasibility of integrating longitudinal CT radiomics with finite element analysis to assess early bone–implant interface changes after 3D-printed titanium limb-salvage reconstruction. This framework may provide a noninvasive approach for postoperative monitoring and implant-interface assessment, although validation in larger cohorts is required.

title: Efficacy of 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography in anticipating the progression of vascular graft and endograft infection: A retrospective multicenter study
abstract: Abstract Background Vascular graft and endograft infection (VGEI) is a life-threatening complication. In this study, we evaluated the efficacy of 18 F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography ( 18 F-FDG-PET/CT) in anticipating the clinical progression of VGEI in patients presenting with fever of unknown origin (FUO) after aortic surgery. Methods This retrospective multicenter study enrolled 29 patients with FUO after aortic surgery (2012–2020). Patients underwent FDG-PET/CT upon admission; the SUV max at the site of the greatest pathological uptake surrounding the graft was measured. The primary endpoint was progression to "proven VGEI," defined by the Management of Aortic Graft Infection Collaboration criteria. Independent predictors of VGEI progression were identified using multivariable Cox regression. Results The median follow-up period was 771 [172–1418] days; the median interval from PET/CT to VGEI diagnosis was 19 [5–60] days. Progression to VGEI was observed in 13 patients (44.8%). Multivariable analysis identified SUV max surrounding the graft as the sole independent predictor of VGEI progression (hazard ratio: 1.40; 95% confidence interval: 1.04–1.89). Receiver operating characteristic analysis revealed an optimal SUV max cut-off of 6.675 (area under the curve = 0.937; sensitivity 100%, specificity 87.5%). In the High-SUV max group ( ≧ 6.675, n = 15), 13 patients (86.7%) experienced VGEI progression, 10 underwent surgical intervention, and six died from VGEI-related causes. Conversely, no patients in the Low-SUV max group (< 6.675) exhibited VGEI progression or VGEI-related death. Conclusions 18 F-FDG-PET/CT is highly effective in predicting the clinical progression of VGEI. High FDG uptake strongly reveals a high risk of advancement, indicating that early surgical intervention should be considered to prevent catastrophic complications.

title: Erdheim–Chester disease with cardiac involvement confirmed by biopsy: a case report
abstract: Abstract Background： Erdheim–Chester disease (ECD) is a rare non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis which manifests as uncontrolled proliferation and infiltration across multiple systems. Cardiovascular involvement is quite common, which is associated with poor prognosis. However, patients often lack prominent cardiovascular symptoms, making diagnosis difficult. Most published cardiac ECD diagnoses rely solely on imaging findings; cases with histopathological confirmation via cardiac tissue biopsy remain extremely scarce. Case presentation: This report describes a 44-year-old woman with 6-month recurrent fevers, multiple prior admissions. Positron Emission Tomography–Computed Tomography (PET-CT) showed a progressive increase in fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) uptake in the soft tissue surrounding the right atrium; echocardiography detected a circumferential heterogeneous mass on the right heart wall plus pericardial effusion. Open cardiac biopsy confirmed non-Langerhans histiocytic proliferation. NGS found MAP2K1 mutation without BRAF V600E alteration, and bone scan showed long bone uptake, verifying ECD. The patient is currently receiving interferon-α (IFN-α) therapy. Conclusions: This is a case of cardiac ECD that was pathologically diagnosed through an open cardiac biopsy. Through the summary of this case and a concise review of cases of ECD with cardiac involvement, we can enhance the understanding of the potential clinical, imaging, and histopathological manifestations of this rare disease, thereby reducing the rates of misdiagnosis and missed diagnosis.

title: Cascade Deep Learning (nnU-Net + ResNet-18) for Meniscus Segmentation and Three-Grade Injury Classification on Knee MRI: A Single-Centre Study with Reader Assistance Evaluation
abstract: Abstract Background Accurate detection and grading of meniscal injury guide treatment, but MRI interpretation is time-consuming and subject to interobserver variability. We developed and evaluated a cascade deep-learning framework that segments the menisci and grades their status (healthy, degenerative, grade-III tear) on knee MRI, and assessed its value as a reader-assistance tool. Methods In this single-centre retrospective study, 562 patients (608 knees; 1,216 coronal and sagittal sequences) scanned on a 1.5-T system between 2018 and 2022 were included. A 3D nnU-Net segmented the medial and lateral menisci. Subsequently, the segmented regions of interest were classified by a 2D ResNet-18 into three grades, and coronal and sagittal predictions were fused by a most-severe-class rule.The dataset was partitioned at the patient level into an 80% training set and a 20% held-out test set. Model performance was evaluated using the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), accuracy, F1 score, and the area under the ROC curve (AUC). In a multi-reader study, two junior readers diagnosed 100 cases, first unaided and subsequently, following a two-week washout period, with AI assistance (probabilities and Grad-CAM maps). Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity for grade-III tears, reading time, and inter-reader agreement were compared using the McNemar test and Cohen’s κ. Results The nnU-Net achieved a mean Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.84 for intact menisci, but only 0.32–0.40 for injured menisci. For binary detection (torn vs. non-torn), the fusion model reached an accuracy of 73.77% (F1-score: 72.88%), with the coronal plane outperforming the sagittal plane (F1-score: 76.29% vs. 68.83%; AUC: 0.79 vs. 0.71); the three-grade accuracy was 68.01%. With AI assistance, the accuracy of junior readers increased from 64.0% to 78.0% (McNemar χ² = 7.68, P < 0.01), sensitivity for grade-III tears improved from 60.0% to 80.0%, reading time decreased by 38% (from 44.7 ± 11.2 to 27.9 ± 7.4 s/case), and interobserver agreement improved from κ = 0.52 to 0.68. Conclusion The cascade nnU-Net + ResNet-18 framework performed meniscus segmentation and injury grading with moderate standalone accuracy but demonstrated a clear assistive benefit, improving the sensitivity and efficiency of junior readers. This framework may serve as a decision-support tool rather than a replacement for expert interpretation.

title: Early Multisystem Presentation of Frank-ter Haar Syndrome with a Novel Compound Heterozygous SH3PXD2B Variant: A Case Report
abstract: Abstract Background: Frank-ter Haar syndrome (FTHS; OMIM #249420) is an ultra-rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic variants in SH3PXD2B, which encodes the podosome adaptor protein TKS4[1]. Fewer than 50 molecularly confirmed cases have been reported. Case presentation: We describe a 6-year-old girl, born at term to non-consanguineous parents, who had low-set ears and craniofacial dysmorphism at birth. A neonatal skull radiograph showed a copper-beaten calvarium, and abdominal ultrasonography incidentally noted bowel-wall thickening; no diagnosis was reached at the time, and echocardiography was normal. At 6 years she presented with global developmental delay, mild intellectual disability, and recurrent lower respiratory tract infections. A repeat skeletal survey confirmed brachycephaly and a persistent copper-beaten skull, with an incidental asymmetry of carpal ossification not previously described in this condition. Paroxysmal inconsolable crying prompted ophthalmological review, which revealed bilateral glaucoma with significant refractive error. Chest radiography and CT thorax were normal. Whole-exome sequencing identified a novel missense variant in SH3PXD2B (exon 13; c.2690C>T, p.(Ser897Phe)) in trans with a paternally inherited nonsense variant (c.1219C>T, p.(Arg407*)), confirmed by segregation and consistent with autosomal recessive FTHS. Conclusions: This case expands the mutational spectrum of SH3PXD2B and shows that non-specific neonatal radiological findings may antedate the recognisable FTHS phenotype by years. Paroxysmal crying as the presenting sign of occult glaucoma underscores the need for proactive ophthalmological screening in skeletal dysplasia syndromes. Trial Registration Not applicable.

title: Uncovering neural decisions: How textual interpretation bridges AI and clinical reasoning
abstract: Abstract Medical imaging artificial intelligence (AI) can achieve strong diagnostic performance, yet its decision evidence often remains difficult to verify, raising concerns about reliability and safety in clinical use. Conventional heatmaps mainly localize model-attended lesion regions and have limited capacity to distinguish multiple overlapping clinical features, whereas image-text explanations may describe the image content without being coupled to the actual decision pathway of the target model. Here, we present CRysTal, a neuron-level post-hoc explanation framework that maps decision-related neuronal activations to standardized clinical terminology through two-stage non-negative sparse regression and cross-category fusion. In breast ultrasound diagnosis, CRysTal linked neurons from EfficientNet-B0, ResNet-50, VGG-19, and ViT-B models to BI-RADS concepts, generating explanations that were more consistent with radiology reports than large-model reasoning, CLIP-Dissect, and linear explanation baselines while preserving the original classification performance. Across the four diagnostic models, CRysTal improved feature-level agreement by 3.4-12.2% and tendency-level agreement by 3.5-19.2% over the second-best baseline. CRysTal further tracked a shift in model explanations during training, from non-specific visual cues toward clinical concepts commonly used by physicians, with concept alignment positively associated with diagnostic performance in ResNet-50 and EfficientNet-B0 (Pearson r = 0.89 and 0.84, respectively). Its reasoning conflict (RCF) score identified erroneous AI predictions with an AUC of 0.745, outperforming saliency-map-based risk signals (AUC range, 0.542-0.625) and a concept bottleneck model (AUC = 0.643). In a reader study involving 20 ultrasound physicians, CRysTal explanations received mean scores close to 97 for explanation accuracy, readability and guideline concordance, and reduced mean reading time by 10.7% for junior physicians and 4.7% for senior experts. Generalization experiments on external breast ultrasound, thyroid ultrasound and dermoscopy datasets provide initial evidence that CRysTal can support auditable AI explanations across standardized medical imaging terminology systems.

In breast ultrasound diagnosis, CRysTal linked neurons from EfficientNet-B0, ResNet-50, VGG-19, and ViT-B models to BI-RADS concepts, generating explanations that were more consistent with radiology reports than large-model reasoning, CLIP-Dissect, and linear explanation baselines while preserving the original classification performance. Across the four diagnostic models, CRysTal improved feature-level agreement by 3.4-12.2% and tendency-level agreement by 3.5-19.2% over the second-best baseline. CRysTal further tracked a shift in model explanations during training, from non-specific visual cues toward clinical concepts commonly used by physicians, with concept alignment positively associated with diagnostic performance in ResNet-50 and EfficientNet-B0 (Pearson r = 0.89 and 0.84, respectively). Its reasoning conflict (RCF) score identified erroneous AI predictions with an AUC of 0.745, outperforming saliency-map-based risk signals (AUC range, 0.542-0.625) and a concept bottleneck model (AUC = 0.643). In a reader study involving 20 ultrasound physicians, CRysTal explanations received mean scores close to 97 for explanation accuracy, readability and guideline concordance, and reduced mean reading time by 10.7% for junior physicians and 4.7% for senior experts. Generalization experiments on external breast ultrasound, thyroid ultrasound and dermoscopy datasets provide initial evidence that CRysTal can support auditable AI explanations across standardized medical imaging terminology systems.

title: Hippocampal surface analysis using discrete Ricci flow and Riemannian metrics for the diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease
abstract: Abstract Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disorder that is characterized by structural changes of the hippocampus, thus hippocampal morphology becomes an important biomarker for early diagnosis. We propose a geometry-aware framework for AD classification based on discrete Ricci flow and Symmetric Positive Definite (SPD) manifold learning. We conformally parameterize the hippocampus surface meshes from the MRI data using Ricci flow and retrieve three geometric descriptors, Heat Kernel Signature, Area Distortion and Conformal Factor, during the Ricci energy optimization process. These features are represented as covariance matrices, resulting in SPD descriptors per subject. To preserve intrinsic manifold structure, classification is performed by KNN with multiple SPD-aware metrics, including the Affine-Invariant Riemannian Metric (AIRM), Wasserstein Metric, Log-Euclidean Metric and so on. Experimental results on ADNI dataset show that AIRM achieves the best performance with 96\% accuracy, which outperforms other metrics evaluated. The results demonstrate that the combination of geometric analysis based on Ricci flow and manifold learning is effective for the diagnosis of Alzheimer’s disease.
